slides.subtitle: AI in Risk Management
slides.narration: Welcome back to the Certified AI Finance Leader program by the Virginia Institute of Finance and Management. In Module Three, we turn our attention to one of the highest-impact areas of AI adoption in financial services: risk management. Across three lessons, you will learn how AI is reshaping risk modeling and scoring, enabling real-time fraud detection and compliance monitoring, and powering next-generation scenario analysis and stress testing. This first lesson focuses on AI-based risk modeling, tracing the evolution from traditional scorecards to machine learning-driven approaches, and addressing the critical challenges of model explainability and regulatory compliance that every finance leader must navigate.

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > AI-Based Risk Modeling and Scoring
slides.narration: Let us begin with Lesson One: AI-Based Risk Modeling and Scoring. Risk modeling is the quantitative backbone of financial risk management. For decades, institutions relied on linear statistical methods and expert-built scorecards. Today, machine learning and deep learning models are fundamentally changing what is possible. In this lesson, we will define what AI risk modeling is and why it matters, trace the evolution of credit scoring from FICO to gradient boosting, compare the major types of risk models in use today, examine the crucial issue of model explainability, and conclude with the regulatory landscape that governs AI in risk. By the end, you will understand both the power and the constraints of deploying AI for risk assessment.

slides.label: The AI Risk Imperative
slides.statement: Financial institutions using AI in risk management report up to 25% reduction in credit losses
slides.sub_text: Source: McKinsey Global Institute, AI in Banking Risk Management, 2023
slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > AI-Based Risk Modeling and Scoring
slides.narration: Consider the financial impact: McKinsey's research on AI adoption in banking risk management shows that institutions deploying machine learning models for credit risk assessment have achieved up to a twenty-five percent reduction in credit losses compared to those relying on traditional scorecards. This is not merely an incremental improvement. When applied across a portfolio of tens of billions of dollars in lending exposure, that twenty-five percent translates to hundreds of millions in avoided losses. The improvement comes from AI's ability to detect subtle, non-linear patterns in borrower behavior that traditional logistic regression models simply cannot capture.

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > AI-Based Risk Modeling and Scoring
slides.narration: The history of credit scoring is a story of increasing sophistication. In 1956, Fair Isaac and Company introduced the FICO score, a logistic regression model built on five variables that became the global standard for consumer credit assessment. Through the 1990s, banks developed internal ratings-based models with proprietary behavioral data. The 2008 financial crisis was a watershed moment that exposed the limitations of existing models, leading to Basel III and far more rigorous requirements for model validation and stress testing. Around 2015, machine learning methods, particularly gradient boosted trees and random forests, began consistently outperforming logistic regression in credit default prediction. Today, in the 2020s, deep learning architectures combined with explainable AI techniques like SHAP are enabling models that are both more powerful and more transparent than anything we had before.

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > AI-Based Risk Modeling and Scoring
slides.narration: Let us compare traditional and AI-driven risk models across six dimensions. In terms of technique, traditional models rely on logistic regression and rule-based scorecards, while AI models use gradient boosting, random forests, and neural networks. For feature handling, traditional models typically use ten to thirty manually selected features, whereas AI models can process hundreds or thousands, including automatically engineered interaction terms. On data sources, AI models extend far beyond bureau data to incorporate transaction flows, geospatial signals, and behavioral data. In accuracy, measured by area under the ROC curve, AI models consistently deliver AUC scores between 0.80 and 0.90, compared to 0.70 to 0.78 for traditional approaches. However, the trade-off appears in explainability: traditional logistic regression coefficients are directly interpretable, while AI models require post-hoc techniques like SHAP values for explanation. Regulatory acceptance of AI models is growing but still varies by jurisdiction. The key takeaway is that AI models offer substantial accuracy improvements, but they must be paired with robust explainability frameworks.

slides.narration: AI is being deployed across every category of financial risk. At the center of a modern risk architecture sits an AI risk engine that serves as the enterprise platform. For credit risk, AI models estimate probability of default, loss given default, and exposure at default with far greater precision than traditional methods. Market risk applications include real-time Value at Risk estimation and volatility forecasting using intraday tick data. Operational risk models apply natural language processing to incident reports and audit logs to predict control failures before they occur. Liquidity risk models forecast cash flows and stress test liquidity coverage ratios. Counterparty risk applications estimate credit valuation adjustments and exposure at default across complex derivative portfolios. And concentration risk models use clustering algorithms to detect hidden correlations in portfolios that traditional sector-based analysis would miss. Credit risk remains the most mature application area, accounting for over sixty percent of AI risk model deployments in banking.

slides.label: Explainability Workflow
slides.title: AI Model Explainability Framework
slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > AI-Based Risk Modeling and Scoring
slides.narration: Explainability is not optional in risk management; it is a regulatory requirement. Here is the workflow that leading institutions follow. After training an AI risk model and generating predictions, the team applies explainability techniques such as SHAP, which stands for SHapley Additive exPlanations, or LIME, which stands for Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations. The critical decision point is whether the model's explanations are sufficiently interpretable for regulators and risk officers. If yes, the team generates a feature importance report documenting which variables drive predictions and by how much. If the model is not sufficiently interpretable, the team must simplify the architecture or add monotonicity constraints, then re-analyze. Once interpretability is achieved, the model goes through formal regulatory review and validation before deployment. This cycle ensures that accuracy never comes at the expense of transparency.

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > AI-Based Risk Modeling and Scoring
slides.narration: The regulatory landscape for AI risk models is complex and evolving rapidly. In the United States, the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 guidance requires comprehensive model risk management for any model used in material decision-making, including validation, back-testing, and ongoing performance monitoring. The European Union's AI Act, which came into force in 2024, classifies credit scoring and risk assessment as high-risk AI applications, requiring conformity assessments, human oversight provisions, and detailed technical documentation. The Basel III and IV frameworks mandate specific validation criteria for any internal model used in regulatory capital calculations. And fair lending laws, including the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, require institutions to demonstrate that AI models do not produce discriminatory outcomes and to provide clear adverse action reason codes when credit is denied. Finance leaders must build compliance into their AI risk models from the design stage, not as an afterthought.

Second, the evolution from FICO's logistic regression to modern gradient boosting and deep learning represents a fundamental shift in what risk models can achieve. slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson Two of Module Three in the Certified AI Finance Leader program. In this lesson, we focus on one of the most high-stakes applications of AI in finance: fraud detection and compliance monitoring. Financial fraud costs the global economy over two trillion dollars annually, and regulatory fines for compliance failures have reached record levels. AI is now the primary line of defense. We will explore the machine learning techniques powering modern fraud detection, understand how anomaly detection works in practice, examine real-time monitoring architectures, and see how AI is automating AML and KYC compliance workflows.

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Fraud Detection and Compliance Monitoring
slides.narration: Lesson Two: Fraud Detection and Compliance Monitoring. This lesson is structured around five core themes. First, we will quantify the scale of financial fraud and why traditional rule-based systems are failing. Second, we will examine the AI and machine learning techniques driving modern fraud detection. Third, we will explore anomaly detection in depth as a key capability. Fourth, we will look at real-time monitoring architectures. And fifth, we will discuss how AI is transforming Anti-Money Laundering and Know Your Customer compliance. By the end, you will understand the full technology stack behind AI-powered financial crime prevention.

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Fraud Detection and Compliance Monitoring
slides.narration: The numbers paint a stark picture of why AI in fraud detection is not optional. Global financial fraud costs an estimated two point one trillion dollars annually according to Nasdaq's Verafin report. Traditional rule-based detection systems generate a staggering ninety-five percent false positive rate, meaning that for every genuine alert, investigators must sift through nineteen false ones. PwC's survey reveals that fifty-four percent of fraud cases are now initially detected by AI systems rather than human investigators. And the cost of compliance failure is severe: global AML fines reached four point seven billion dollars in 2023 alone. These statistics make a compelling case that legacy approaches to fraud detection and compliance are unsustainable, and that AI is no longer a competitive advantage but an operational necessity.

slides.label: Detection Pipeline
slides.title: AI Fraud Detection Funnel

stages.label: Total Transactions
stages.description: All transactions processed through the institution's payment and transfer systems across channels

stages.label: Rule-Based Pre-Filter
stages.description: Basic velocity checks, amount thresholds, and geographic rules filter obvious anomalies

stages.label: ML Scoring Engine
stages.description: Gradient boosted models and neural networks assign fraud probability scores based on 200+ features

stages.label: Anomaly Detection Layer
stages.description: Unsupervised isolation forests and autoencoders detect previously unknown fraud patterns

stages.label: Confirmed Fraud
stages.description: Verified fraud cases blocked, reported to authorities, and fed back into model training

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Fraud Detection and Compliance Monitoring
slides.narration: Understanding the modern fraud detection pipeline is essential. Think of it as a funnel that progressively narrows. At the top, a major bank might process over ten million transactions daily. The first layer is a rule-based pre-filter that applies basic velocity checks, amount thresholds, and geographic rules, flagging roughly five hundred thousand transactions for further review. Those flagged transactions pass through a machine learning scoring engine, typically gradient boosted models evaluating over two hundred features, which narrows the pool to about twenty-five thousand high-risk transactions. Next, an unsupervised anomaly detection layer using techniques like isolation forests and autoencoders identifies approximately five thousand confirmed anomalies, including novel fraud patterns the supervised models have never seen. Only about eight hundred cases reach human investigators, who receive AI-generated evidence packages and recommended actions. Of those, approximately two hundred are confirmed as actual fraud. This funnel approach means AI reduces the human investigation burden by over ninety-nine percent while improving detection rates.

slides.label: ML Techniques
slides.title: AI Techniques for Fraud Detection

items.title: Gradient Boosted Trees
items.description: XGBoost and LightGBM models that learn from labeled fraud/non-fraud examples, excelling at tabular transaction data with hundreds of engineered features

items.title: Deep Neural Networks
items.description: Recurrent and transformer architectures that model sequential transaction behavior, detecting patterns across time series of customer activity

items.title: Isolation Forests
items.description: Unsupervised tree-based method that identifies outliers by measuring how easily a data point can be isolated from the rest of the dataset

items.title: Graph Neural Networks
items.description: Network-based models that detect fraud rings and collusion by analyzing relationship patterns between accounts, entities, and transactions

items.title: Autoencoders
items.description: Neural networks trained to reconstruct normal transactions; fraud is detected when reconstruction error exceeds a learned threshold

items.title: Ensemble Stacking
items.description: Meta-learning approach combining predictions from multiple diverse models to achieve higher accuracy and robustness than any single model

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Fraud Detection and Compliance Monitoring
slides.narration: Modern fraud detection employs a diverse toolkit of AI techniques. Gradient boosted tree models like XGBoost and LightGBM remain the workhorses for supervised fraud detection on tabular transaction data, consistently outperforming other methods when labeled training data is available. Deep neural networks, particularly recurrent and transformer architectures, excel at modeling sequential transaction behavior over time. Isolation forests are a powerful unsupervised technique that identifies anomalies by measuring how easily a transaction can be separated from normal patterns, making them effective at catching novel fraud types. Graph neural networks are increasingly important for detecting fraud rings and collusion by analyzing the network of relationships between accounts and entities. Autoencoders learn to reconstruct what normal transactions look like; when a transaction cannot be accurately reconstructed, it is flagged as potentially fraudulent. Finally, ensemble stacking combines predictions from multiple models to achieve greater accuracy and robustness. The most effective fraud detection systems use several of these techniques in combination.

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Fraud Detection and Compliance Monitoring
slides.narration: Let us examine an illustrative case. Nordic Financial Group, a Scandinavian banking consortium managing one hundred and twenty billion dollars in assets, processed eight million card transactions daily through a legacy rule-based system with over three thousand manually maintained rules. The results were unsustainable: a ninety-two percent false positive rate, one hundred and eighty full-time investigators, and an estimated fifteen percent of actual fraud going undetected. After deploying an ensemble of gradient boosted models for supervised scoring and graph neural networks for relationship-based fraud ring detection, the results were transformative. False positives dropped by sixty percent, meaning investigators could focus on genuine threats. The fraud detection rate improved by thirty-five percent, catching sophisticated synthetic identity fraud and collusion schemes that rules could never detect. Combined savings from reduced investigation costs and prevented losses reached forty-seven million dollars annually. The critical lesson is that AI does not just catch more fraud; it fundamentally changes the economics of fraud prevention.

slides.narration: AI is transforming every stage of AML and KYC compliance. In customer due diligence, AI automates identity verification through document OCR and biometric matching, performs real-time sanctions and politically exposed persons screening, and builds dynamic risk profiles that update continuously based on actual transaction behavior rather than static annual reviews. For transaction monitoring, machine learning replaces rigid threshold rules with adaptive behavioral baselines unique to each customer, while network analysis detects complex layering patterns across accounts and NLP extracts context from payment narratives. In suspicious activity reporting, AI auto-generates SAR narratives from investigation findings, cutting filing time from hours to minutes and ensuring consistent quality. For ongoing monitoring and governance, AML models require continuous recalibration as criminal methods evolve. Performance dashboards track precision and recall metrics daily, and regulatory changes automatically trigger revalidation workflows. Together, these capabilities enable compliance teams to shift from reactive processing to proactive risk prevention.

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Fraud Detection and Compliance Monitoring
slides.narration: Let us establish best practices for implementing AI in fraud detection and compliance. On the do side: always combine supervised and unsupervised approaches so you can detect both known fraud patterns and completely novel attack vectors. Ensure real-time scoring with sub-one-hundred-millisecond latency because customers expect instant transaction authorization. Maintain comprehensive audit trails, as regulators will scrutinize every model decision. Retrain models at least quarterly to keep pace with evolving fraud tactics. And build closed feedback loops so that investigator decisions on alerts flow directly back into model training data. On the don't side: never rely solely on supervised models, because they are blind to fraud types not present in historical data. Always bias-test AML models across demographics and geographies before deployment. Avoid using static threshold rules as your primary mechanism; they degrade within months. Do not treat compliance automation purely as a cost center; it should be framed as risk reduction. And never deploy new AI compliance approaches without engaging your regulatory team first.

slides.subtitle: AI in Risk Management
slides.narration: Welcome to the final lesson of Module Three in the Certified AI Finance Leader program. In this lesson, we address one of the most computationally demanding and strategically important applications of AI in finance: scenario analysis and stress testing. Every financial institution must demonstrate to regulators and stakeholders that it can withstand severe but plausible economic shocks. Traditionally, stress testing has been a manual, time-intensive process. AI is transforming it into a dynamic, continuous capability. We will cover the Basel regulatory framework that drives stress testing requirements, Monte Carlo simulation methods, AI-driven scenario generation, and the critical discipline of model risk management.

slides.topic_title: Scenario Analysis and Stress Testing with AI
slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Scenario Analysis and Stress Testing with AI
slides.narration: Lesson Three: Scenario Analysis and Stress Testing with AI. This lesson is organized into four sections. First, we will review the Basel III and IV stress testing frameworks that define the regulatory requirements for capital adequacy testing. Second, we will examine Monte Carlo simulation and why it is the mathematical foundation for modern risk quantification. Third, we will explore how AI generates scenarios that go beyond what human analysts can conceive. And fourth, we will discuss model risk management, the discipline of ensuring that the models themselves do not become a source of risk. By the end, you will understand how AI enables institutions to stress test more scenarios, more frequently, and with greater confidence.

slides.label: Regulatory Hierarchy
slides.title: Basel Stress Testing Framework

levels.label: ICAAP / ILAAP
levels.description: Internal Capital and Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Processes: institution's own forward-looking assessment of capital and liquidity needs under stress

levels.label: Supervisory Stress Tests
levels.description: Regulator-mandated scenarios (CCAR, EBA) testing capital adequacy under severe adverse macroeconomic conditions with prescribed shock parameters

levels.label: Pillar 2 Requirements
levels.description: Institution-specific capital add-ons based on risks not fully captured by Pillar 1, including concentration risk, interest rate risk, and model risk

levels.label: Pillar 1 Minimum Capital
levels.description: Standardized minimum capital requirements: CET1 at 4.5%, Tier 1 at 6%, Total Capital at 8%, plus conservation and countercyclical buffers

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Scenario Analysis and Stress Testing with AI
slides.narration: Stress testing exists within a layered regulatory framework established by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. At the base is Pillar 1, which sets minimum capital requirements: Common Equity Tier 1 at four point five percent, Tier 1 capital at six percent, and total capital at eight percent, plus conservation and countercyclical buffers. The next layer is Pillar 2, which adds institution-specific capital requirements for risks not fully captured by Pillar 1, including concentration risk, interest rate risk in the banking book, and notably, model risk itself. Above that are supervisory stress tests, such as the Fed's Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review in the US and the European Banking Authority's exercises, which test capital adequacy under severely adverse macroeconomic scenarios prescribed by regulators. At the top are ICAAP and ILAAP, the institution's own internal assessments of capital and liquidity adequacy under forward-looking stress scenarios. AI enhances every layer of this framework, but its greatest impact is in making the top two layers more rigorous and comprehensive.

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Scenario Analysis and Stress Testing with AI
slides.narration: Effective stress testing requires a comprehensive scenario matrix organized by two dimensions: probability and severity. In the high-severity, low-probability quadrant, we find tail risk events: pandemic-driven recessions, sovereign defaults, and systemic cyberattacks. These are the hardest to model traditionally and where AI provides the greatest value. In the high-severity, higher-probability quadrant are plausible severe scenarios like major property corrections, rapid interest rate rises, and geopolitical supply chain disruptions. The low-severity, low-probability quadrant contains emerging risks like climate transition impacts, cryptocurrency contagion, and AI-driven market instability. And in the low-severity, higher-probability quadrant are baseline stress scenarios such as mild recessions and gradual credit deterioration. Traditional stress testing typically focuses on only a handful of regulator-prescribed scenarios. AI enables institutions to test across hundreds or thousands of scenarios spanning this entire matrix, providing a far more comprehensive view of their risk exposure.

slides.label: Monte Carlo Methods
slides.title: Monte Carlo Simulation for Risk
slides.step_title: How Monte Carlo Simulation Quantifies Risk
slides.description: Monte Carlo simulation generates thousands to millions of random scenarios based on probability distributions, calculating portfolio outcomes for each. The distribution of outcomes provides risk metrics like VaR and Expected Shortfall.
sub_steps: Define risk factors and their probability distributions (interest rates, FX rates, credit spreads, GDP growth, unemployment)
Specify correlation structures between risk factors using historical covariance matrices or copula models
Generate 10,000 to 1,000,000 random draws from the joint distribution of all risk factors simultaneously
For each draw, revalue the entire portfolio using full repricing models or Taylor approximations
Aggregate the distribution of portfolio outcomes to calculate VaR (e.g., 99th percentile loss) and Expected Shortfall
AI accelerates this process through GPU-parallelized computation and learned surrogate models that replace slow full-repricing steps
slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Scenario Analysis and Stress Testing with AI
slides.narration: Monte Carlo simulation is the mathematical foundation of modern risk quantification. The process works as follows. First, you define the risk factors, such as interest rates, foreign exchange rates, credit spreads, GDP growth, and unemployment, along with their probability distributions based on historical data. Second, you specify the correlation structure between these factors, because risk factors do not move independently. Third, you generate thousands to millions of random draws from the joint distribution of all risk factors simultaneously. Fourth, for each random scenario, you revalue the entire portfolio. Fifth, you aggregate the distribution of outcomes to calculate key risk metrics like Value at Risk at the ninety-ninth percentile and Expected Shortfall. The challenge is computational: a large bank with millions of positions might need to perform billions of repricing calculations. This is where AI makes a transformative contribution. GPU-parallelized computation accelerates the random generation step, and machine learning surrogate models can approximate the expensive full-repricing step, reducing computation time from hours to minutes while maintaining accuracy within acceptable tolerance levels.

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Scenario Analysis and Stress Testing with AI
slides.narration: AI-driven scenario generation transforms stress testing from a periodic regulatory exercise into a continuous strategic capability. The cycle begins with historical analysis, where AI examines decades of macroeconomic, market, and credit data to identify patterns from past stress episodes and regime changes. Next, generative models, specifically Generative Adversarial Networks and Variational Autoencoders, create plausible but novel scenarios that extend beyond what history has shown, including extreme tail events that have never actually occurred but are economically coherent. These generated scenarios then go through a validation step where risk committees assess their plausibility and internal consistency. Validated scenarios are applied to the current portfolio using ML-accelerated repricing engines. The results feed into capital adequacy assessments that determine whether existing buffers exceed regulatory minimums under each scenario. Finally, management designs strategic responses, including hedging strategies and portfolio adjustments, tested against the scenario outcomes. This cycle can run continuously rather than just once or twice a year as traditional stress testing does.

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Scenario Analysis and Stress Testing with AI
slides.narration: Let us compare the two approaches directly. On scenario count, traditional methods test three to ten regulator-prescribed scenarios, while AI enables thousands of scenarios including novel tail risks. On frequency, traditional stress testing is annual or semi-annual, while AI enables continuous or daily testing. Computation time drops from weeks to hours or even minutes with GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo and machine learning surrogate models. For scenario design, traditional approaches rely on expert judgment and historical precedent, while AI generates economically coherent scenarios that may have no historical precedent. And in sensitivity analysis, AI enables comprehensive reverse stress testing, systematically identifying the exact market conditions that would breach capital thresholds, which is computationally infeasible with traditional methods. The verdict is clear: AI-powered stress testing provides orders-of-magnitude improvements in coverage, frequency, and speed, transforming stress testing from a backward-looking compliance exercise into a forward-looking strategic capability.

slides.breadcrumb: CAIFL > Module 03 > Scenario Analysis and Stress Testing with AI
slides.narration: As institutions deploy more AI models for risk management, the discipline of model risk management becomes critical. The risk that models themselves produce incorrect outputs is a meta-risk that must be explicitly managed. This roadmap outlines four phases. Phase one is model inventory and classification. Every AI model must be cataloged with clear ownership, purpose, and risk tier. Tier 1 models affecting regulatory capital require the most rigorous governance. Phase two establishes a validation and testing framework. An independent validation team, separate from the developers, conducts back-testing, benchmarking, and champion-challenger comparisons before any model enters production. Phase three focuses on ongoing monitoring and governance. Real-time dashboards track accuracy, stability, and drift metrics, with automatic triggers for revalidation when performance degrades. A model risk committee has authority to approve, restrict, or retire models. Phase four is continuous improvement: integrating model risk into the enterprise risk appetite framework, conducting annual model risk stress tests, and benchmarking against regulatory expectations and industry peers.

slides.narration: Let us recap Lesson Three. First, the Basel III and IV frameworks establish the layered regulatory requirements for stress testing, from Pillar 1 minimum capital ratios through supervisory stress tests and ICAAP, and AI enhances the rigor and comprehensiveness of every layer. Second, Monte Carlo simulation provides the mathematical foundation for modern risk quantification, and AI dramatically accelerates it through GPU-parallelized computation and learned surrogate models that replace expensive full-repricing calculations. Third, AI-driven scenario generation using Generative Adversarial Networks and Variational Autoencoders creates thousands of economically coherent scenarios beyond historical experience, transforming stress testing from a periodic exercise into a continuous strategic capability. And fourth, as AI model deployment scales, model risk management through independent validation, real-time monitoring, and strong governance becomes essential to ensure that the models themselves do not become a source of risk. This concludes Module Three on AI in Risk Management.

That wraps up Lesson Three and the entirety of Module Three: AI in Risk Management. Across these three lessons, you have built a comprehensive understanding of how AI transforms risk modeling and credit scoring, how it powers real-time fraud detection and automated compliance monitoring, and how it enables sophisticated scenario analysis and stress testing. These capabilities are not theoretical; they are being deployed by leading financial institutions today, delivering measurable improvements in risk detection, capital efficiency, and regulatory compliance. In the next module, we will shift our focus to AI ethics, governance, and the responsible deployment of these powerful technologies. See you there.
